about: Introduction to Fundamentals of Clinical Science 1 (MBBS0017) is the one-week Introduction and Orientation Module that opens UCL's MBBS Year 1. It is taught in person in Term 1 (28 September to 2 October 2026 in the 2026–27 timetable) and carries 0 credits. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue says it orients students to a year built from consecutive, systems-based modules with integrated teaching, alongside Clinical and Professional Practice modules that run through all six years. The catalogue lists no learning outcomes or separate assessment for the week, so this guide explains how Year 1 is organised and how to prepare; it does not invent a syllabus.

Setting up your learning for an integrated course

notes.h: What the Introduction and Orientation week is
notes.body:
Introduction to Fundamentals of Clinical Science 1 (MBBS0017) is not a taught science module with its own syllabus. It is the one-week Introduction and Orientation Module (often shortened to IOM) that opens UCL's MBBS Year 1.

What UCL's official pages say
- The 2026/27 module catalogue describes it as a one-week introduction and orientation module to Year 1. It is taught in person in Term 1, carries 0 credits and is open only to MBBS students.
- The catalogue explains that Year 1 is built from consecutive, systems-based modules, each building on the ones before and each centred on a physiological system, with teaching integrated across disciplines. Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP) modules run alongside them throughout the six-year programme.
- The catalogue entry does not list learning outcomes or a separate assessment method for the week.
- UCL's 2026–27 overall timetable places the Year 1 IOM in the week of 28 September to 2 October 2026, immediately before Foundations of Health and Medical Practice.

What the week has traditionally included
UCL's older Year 1 study guide (2018–19, so check current arrangements on Moodle) described the introductory week as giving an overview of the MBBS programme, a chance to meet fellow students, staff and faculty, a small amount of course material and key information, and an introduction to in-course and end-of-year assessment. Expect the current week to cover similar ground, but rely on your own timetable for details.

Why the name matters
The module's name reflects the fact that Years 1 and 2 at UCL are called Fundamentals of Clinical Science 1 and 2. UCL's Year 1 programme page describes Year 1 as a systems-based learning experience in the basic clinical sciences, aiming to build understanding of science as it applies to clinical medicine, data analysis, research and report-writing skills, early patient contact and professional skills, the ethical, social and legal aspects of medicine, and preparation for the integrated BSc in Year 3.

How to get the most from the week
- Find your bearings: the main teaching sites, Moodle pages for Year 1 and each module, your timetable, and how to contact the Year 1 team.
- Meet your personal tutor and tutor group if these are introduced, and learn where to go for support (UCL's Year 1 pages list contacts for curriculum queries, assessment queries and Medical Student Support).
- Read the key documents you are pointed to, especially the Year 1 format of assessments, the policies for MBBS assessments and the MBBS Mark Scheme.
- Set up your study system before the first systems module starts: a calendar, a note-taking method and a flashcard or question bank routine.
- Start conversations with classmates; study groups formed early often last through the course.

What not to worry about
The week is not assessed by an exam, and you are not expected to know medical content yet. Its value lies in understanding how the year works so that nothing about the structure surprises you later.

Exam tips: there is no exam for this week, but note the key dates (formative papers and the two Applied Knowledge Tests) and the documents that set the rules for them as soon as you receive them.

UCL's Year 1 programme page lists the modules in this order. Knowing the shape of the year helps you see where each lecture fits.

Horizontal (systems-based) modules, taught one after another
- Introduction to Fundamentals of Clinical Science 1 (MBBS0017): the orientation week.
- Foundations of Health and Medical Practice (MBBS0013): core knowledge and an introduction to learning in medicine (in 2026–27, four weeks in October).
- Infection and Defence (MBBS0014): microbes, immunity, epidemiology and anti-infective drugs (in 2026–27, four weeks in November).
- Circulation and Breathing (MBBS0015): the cardiovascular and respiratory systems (December to early February).
- Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism (MBBS0016): later in the year.

Consolidation, Integration and Feedback (CIF) weeks
- Weeks A, B and C (MBBS0020, MBBS0021, MBBS0022) follow the systems modules and are for consolidating and integrating what you have learned, with feedback.
- UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments describes online formative papers in the November and February CIF weeks, the February one taken as a mock under exam conditions.

Vertical modules, running through the year
- Patient Pathway – Integrated and Community Care (MBBS0041): the first of four patient pathways, with community visits and meetings with patients and carers.
- MBBS0042: Anatomy and Imaging, Clinical Skills (and Practical Procedures), Doctor as a Data Scientist, Pathological Sciences and Use of Medicines.
- MBBS0047: Mental Health, Social Determinants of Health, Clinical Communication, Ethics and Law, Patient Safety, and Professionalism.
- The UCLMS Toolkit (MBBS0077) and the Student Selected Component (MBBS0078).

'Horizontal' and 'vertical'
Horizontal modules are time-limited blocks centred on a body system. Vertical modules are themes that run across the year and through all six years, so that, for example, anatomy, pharmacology principles and ethics come up within every system block.

How Year 1 is assessed (2026–27)
- The summative assessment is described by UCL as an integrated written and practical assessment made up of two Applied Knowledge Tests: Paper 1 (MBBS0084) and Paper 2 (MBBS0085). Each is a 2-hour online paper of no more than 100 marks, mixing single best answer and very short answer questions, some with images. There is no negative marking.
- The papers are blueprinted to the year of study, the MBBS Curriculum Map and the GMC's standards, and test application of knowledge across modules rather than one module at a time.
- UCL's assessment dates document (May 2026 version) lists formative papers in the week commencing 30 November 2026 and on 9 February 2027, and the summative AKT 1 and AKT 2 on 18 and 20 May 2027. Dates can change, so check the latest version.
- The 2026–27 MBBS Mark Scheme says that progression from Year 1 requires completing the prescribed course, sign-off for required modules and placements, and submission of a portfolio, as well as passing the examinations.

What this means for you
- Every systems module feeds into the same end-of-year papers, so keep earlier modules alive with regular review.
- Use the CIF weeks to find gaps, not just to rest.

Exam tips: learn the order of the modules and which ones are vertical; questions in the AKTs integrate across them, so you should be able to link, say, infection with anatomy, pharmacology principles and ethics.

From your first day you are a medical student, and the General Medical Council (GMC) expects you to behave professionally on and off campus. The orientation week is the right time to understand what that means.

The GMC's standards
- Good medical practice is the GMC's core guidance for doctors. The current version came into effect on 30 January 2024 and is organised into four domains: knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; and trust and professionalism.
- Achieving good medical practice: guidance for medical students applies these standards to students. Its themes include creating fair and compassionate workplaces, tackling discrimination, treating patients fairly, patient-centred care, consent and confidentiality, taking care of your own wellbeing, communicating as a medical student, and engaging with processes and policies.
- UCL's Year 1 assessments are blueprinted against the GMC's Good medical practice and Outcomes for graduates as relevant to Year 1, so professionalism is examined, not just encouraged.

Core behaviours to start now
- Honesty and integrity in everything, including attendance records, coursework and examinations. Plagiarism and collusion are professional issues as well as academic ones.
- Confidentiality: do not discuss identifiable patients in public places or online; anonymise anything you write about patient encounters, including reflections.
- Social media: what you post is public and permanent; the same standards apply online as in person.
- Introduce yourself as a medical student, explain your role and accept that patients may decline to see you.
- Treat everyone with respect, including patients, colleagues, staff and fellow students, and challenge or report bullying, harassment and discrimination.
- Know your limits: never give clinical advice beyond your competence.
- Look after your health and seek help early; using support is a sign of insight, not weakness.

Fitness to practise
Medical schools have procedures for concerns about students' fitness to practise, which can arise from issues such as dishonesty, persistent unprofessional behaviour or criminal convictions. Most concerns are about behaviour and are dealt with supportively, but serious or repeated problems can affect your progress. Being open about mistakes and engaging with support counts in your favour.

Raising concerns
If you see something that might put a patient at risk, you should raise it, normally first with your supervisor or tutor. UCL and NHS organisations have routes for doing this.

Where to find help
UCL's Year 1 pages list contacts for curriculum and assessment queries, and Medical Student Support for personal and academic difficulties. Your personal tutor is another first port of call.

Exam tips: in professionalism questions, the best answer usually puts patient safety first, is honest, respects confidentiality, and escalates concerns to the right person rather than acting alone or ignoring them.

notes.h: Setting up your learning for an integrated course
notes.body:
Medicine at UCL is integrated: each systems module mixes anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, pathology, pharmacology principles, clinical skills and the social sciences, and the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests ask you to apply all of them together. How you study from week one matters more than how many hours you spend.

Work from learning objectives
- Each session and module on Moodle has learning objectives. These are the closest thing to a syllabus and are what assessments are mapped to.
- After each day, check that you can answer each objective in your own words without notes.

Use methods with good evidence
- Retrieval practice: test yourself with questions and flashcards rather than rereading. Recalling information strengthens memory far more than recognising it. Very short answer questions in particular reward recall.
- Spaced practice: revisit material after a day, a week and a month, rather than cramming once.
- Interleaving: mix topics in practice sessions, which mirrors integrated exam questions.
- Elaboration: ask how and why; link new ideas to what you already know and to clinical examples.
- A widely cited review by Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) rated practice testing and distributed practice as the most useful of the common study techniques, and highlighting and rereading as of low utility.

Make links across disciplines
For each condition you meet, sketch a quick map: normal structure and function, what goes wrong, how it presents, how it is investigated, the principles of treatment, and the patient's experience and social context. This is exactly the integration the AKTs test.

Organise your time
- Keep a weekly plan with lectures, practicals, placements, Patient Pathway visits and Student Selected Component sessions (Thursday afternoons in Year 1, according to the 2026–27 overall timetable).
- Build in time to review previous modules every week, so that by the end of the year you are revising, not relearning.
- Protect sleep, exercise and social time; they improve memory and wellbeing.

Use feedback and formatives
- The CIF weeks give you formative papers in the same question types as the summative tests. Treat them seriously and analyse each error: knowledge gap, misreading, poor technique or timing.
- Discuss difficulties with your personal tutor early.

Study groups
Small groups that quiz each other, explain topics aloud and write practice questions work well. Writing a question with plausible wrong answers is a demanding test of understanding.

Common early mistakes
- Trying to write down every word of every lecture.
- Leaving review until the CIF week or the end of the year.
- Relying on outside resources that do not match UCL's learning objectives.

Exam tips: from the first systems module, end each week with a short mixed quiz covering this week and earlier weeks; that habit is the best preparation for an integrated end-of-year exam.

questions.q: In UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 timetable, which module comes straight after the one-week Introduction and Orientation Module?
options: Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week A
Foundations of Health and Medical Practice
Patient Pathway – Integrated and Community Care
questions.why: Foundations of Health and Medical Practice follows the orientation week and runs through October. Infection and Defence is the next systems module after Foundations, in November, so choosing it skips a module. CIF Week A comes after the systems modules it consolidates, not at the start of the year. The Patient Pathway is a vertical module running alongside the year, not a block that follows the orientation week.

questions.q: How are UCL's Clinical and Professional Practice (CPP) modules organised in relation to the systems-based modules?
options: Only in the clinical years, from Year 4 onwards
As a separate block taught after all the systems modules in Term 3
As vertical modules running alongside the systems modules throughout the six-year programme
questions.why: UCL describes CPP modules as running throughout the six-year programme, alongside each year's systems-based modules. They are not saved for a block at the end of the year; that idea comes from picturing them as a separate subject rather than integrated themes. They start in Year 1, not only in the clinical years, as the Year 1 module list (MBBS0041, MBBS0042, MBBS0047) shows. The Student Selected Component is a separate module; CPP teaching is core, not optional.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four domains of the GMC's Good medical practice (2024)?
questions.why: 'Safety and quality' was a domain of the previous (2013) edition of Good medical practice, so it is the one that is not a 2024 domain. The 2024 domains are knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; and trust and professionalism, so the other three options are all current domains.

questions.q: Explain the difference between horizontal and vertical modules in UCL's MBBS Year 1, giving two examples of each.
markScheme: Horizontal: time-limited, sequential, systems-based blocks with integrated teaching
Examples of horizontal: any two of Foundations of Health and Medical Practice, Infection and Defence, Circulation and Breathing, Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism
Vertical: themes running across the year and through all six years (CPP)

Examples of vertical: any two of the Patient Pathway, Anatomy and Imaging, Clinical Skills, Doctor as a Data Scientist, Pathological Sciences, Use of Medicines, Clinical Communication, Ethics and Law, Mental Health, Professionalism, etc.
questions.modelAnswer: Horizontal modules are time-limited blocks taught one after another, each centred on a body system with teaching integrated across disciplines; examples are Infection and Defence and Circulation and Breathing. Vertical modules are themes that run across the whole year and continue through all six years of the programme, so they appear within every systems block; examples are the Patient Pathway – Integrated and Community Care and the Clinical and Professional Practice strands such as Anatomy and Imaging or Ethics and Law.
